'''Lubert Stryer''' (March 2, 1938 – April 8, 2024) was an American academic who was the Emeritus Mrs. George A. Winzer Professor of [[Cell Biology]], at [[Stanford University School of Medicine]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://med.stanford.edu/profiles/Lubert_Stryer/|title=Lubert Stryer}}</ref><ref name="amphilsoc.org">{{cite web |url=http://www.amphilsoc.org/public-profile/C27D90EF-D697-DE11-A8C4-0013724C588C |title=Our Apologies &#124; American Philosophical Society |access-date=2012-03-10 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120720035547/http://www.amphilsoc.org/public-profile/C27D90EF-D697-DE11-A8C4-0013724C588C |archive-date=2012-07-20 }}</ref> His research over more than four decades had been centered on the interplay of light and life. In 2006 he received the [[National Medal of Science]] from [[George W. Bush|President Bush]] at a ceremony at the White House for elucidating the biochemical basis of signal amplification in vision, pioneering the development of high density [[microarray]]s for [[genetic analysis]], and authoring the standard undergraduate biochemistry textbook, ''[[Biochemistry (book)|Biochemistry]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=109741|title=President to Award 2005-2006 National Medals of Science and National Medals of Technology Honoring Nation's Leading Researchers, Inventors and Innovators - NSF - National Science Foundation}}</ref> It is now in its tenth edition and also edited by [[Jeremy M. Berg|Jeremy Berg]], Justin Hines, John L. Tymoczko and Gregory J. Gatto, Jr.<ref name="Biochemistry 10">{{cite book|last1=Stryer|title=Biochemistry|date=2023|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|isbn=978-1319498504|edition=10|display-authors=etal}}</ref>

Stryer received his B.S. degree from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1957 and his M.D. degree from [[Harvard Medical School]]. He was a [[Helen Hay Whitney Foundation|Helen Hay Whitney]] Research Fellow<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hhwf.org/cgi/DirScript.cgi |title=Archived copy |access-date=2012-04-01 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121114211717/http://www.hhwf.org/cgi/DirScript.cgi |archive-date=2012-11-14 }}</ref> in the department of physics at Harvard and then at the [[MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www2.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/about-lmb/archiveservice/alumni/s|title=Alumni - MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology|work=MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology}}</ref> in [[Cambridge]], England, before joining the faculty of the department of biochemistry at [[Stanford]] in 1963. In 1969 he moved to [[Yale University|Yale]] to become Professor of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry, and in 1976, he returned to Stanford to head a new Department of Structural Biology.<ref name="amphilsoc.org"/><ref name="Everything is illuminated: ‘Reflections’ on light and life by Lubert Stryer">{{cite web|last1=McCarthy|first1=Pumtiwitt|title=Everything is illuminated: 'Reflections' on light and life by Lubert Stryer|url=http://www.asbmb.org/asbmbtoday/asbmbtoday_article.aspx?id=18029|publisher=[[American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology]]|access-date=19 June 2016}}</ref>

Stryer died in Stanford, California April 8, 2024, at the age of 86.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2024/05/lubert-stryer--luminary-scientist-of-light-and-life--author-of-c.html |title=Lubert Stryer, luminary scientist of light and life, author of classic textbook, dies at 86 |first1=Nina |last1=Bai |date=May 1, 2024 |publisher=Stanford Medicine |access-date=May 4, 2024}}</ref>

==Research profile==
Stryer and coworkers pioneered the use of fluorescence spectroscopy, particularly [[Förster resonance energy transfer]] (FRET), to monitor the structure and dynamics of biological macromolecules.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Stryer | first1 = L | year = 1968 | title = Fluorescence spectroscopy of proteins | journal = Science | volume = 1632 | issue = 3853| pages = 526–533 | doi = 10.1126/science.162.3853.526 | pmid = 5706935 | bibcode = 1968Sci...162..526S }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://probes.invitrogen.com/resources/whatsnew/pressrelease/051302.html |title=Invitrogen - Molecular Probes - Press Release |access-date=2010-10-18 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110614115755/http://probes.invitrogen.com/resources/whatsnew/pressrelease/051302.html |archive-date=2011-06-14 }}</ref> In 1967, Stryer and [[Dick Haugland|Haugland]] showed that the efficiency of energy transfer depends on the inverse sixth power of the distance between the donor and acceptor,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Stryer | first1 = L. | last2 = Haugland | first2 = R.P. | year = 1967 | title = Energy transfer: a spectroscopic ruler | journal = Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA | volume = 58 | issue = 2| pages = 719–725 | doi=10.1073/pnas.58.2.719 | pmid=5233469 | pmc=335693| bibcode = 1967PNAS...58..719S | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>Lakowicz, J.R., 2006. ''Principles of Fluorescence Spectroscopy'' (Springer, 3rd ed., p. 449)</ref> as predicted by Förster's theory. They proposed that energy transfer can serve as a spectroscopic ruler to reveal proximity relationships in biological macromolecules.

A second contribution was Stryer's discovery of the primary stage of amplification in visual excitation.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Fung | first1 = B. | last2 = Hurley | first2 = J.B. | last3 = Stryer | first3 = L. | year = 1981 | title = Flow of information in the light-triggered cyclic nucleotide cascade of vision | journal = Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA | volume = 78 | issue = 1| pages = 152–156 | doi=10.1073/pnas.78.1.152 | pmid=6264430 | pmc=319009| bibcode = 1981PNAS...78..152F | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://pubs.acs.org/isubscribe/journals/cen/85/i29/html/8529awards.html|title=Chemical & Engineering News - Serving the chemical, life sciences and laboratory worlds}}</ref> Stryer, together with Fung and Hurley, showed that a single photoexcited rhodopsin molecule activates many molecules of transducin, which in turn activate many molecules of a cyclic GMP phosphodiesterase. Stryer's laboratory has also contributed to our understanding of the role of calcium in visual recovery and adaptation.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Koch | first1 = K.-W. | last2 = Stryer | first2 = L. | year = 1988 | title = Highly cooperative feedback control of retinal rod guanylate cyclase by calcium ion | journal = Nature | volume = 334 | issue = 6177| pages = 64–66 | doi=10.1038/334064a0 | pmid=2455233| bibcode = 1988Natur.334...64K | s2cid = 4253998 }}</ref><ref><Ames, J.B., Ishima, R., Tanaka, T., Gordon, J.I., Stryer, L., Ikura, M., 1997. Molecular mechanics of calcium-myristoyl switches. ''Nature'' 389:198-202</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Burgoyne | first1 = R.D. | last2 = Weiss | first2 = J.L. | year = 2001 | title = The neuronal calcium sensor family of Ca2+-binding proteins | journal = Biochem. J. | volume = 353 | issue = Pt 1| pages = 1–12 | doi=10.1042/bj3530001| pmid = 11115393 | pmc = 1221537 }}</ref>

Stryer participated in developing light-directed, spatially addressable parallel chemical synthesis for the synthesis of peptides and polynucleotides.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Fodor | first1 = S.P.A. | last2 = Read | first2 = J.L. | last3 = Pirrung | first3 = M.C. | last4 = Stryer | first4 = L. | last5 = Lu | first5 = A.T. | last6 = Solas | first6 = D. | year = 1991 | title = Light-directed, spatially addressable parallel chemical synthesis | journal = Science | volume = 251 | issue = 4995| pages = 767–773 | doi=10.1126/science.1990438 | pmid=1990438| bibcode = 1991Sci...251..767F }}</ref><ref>Fodor, S.P.A., Pirrung, M.C., Read, J.L., and Stryer, L., Array of oligonucleotides on a solid substrate. U.S. Patent No. 5,445,934. Issued August 29, 1995</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aaas.org/aboutaaas/awards/newcomb/newcomb2007.shtml|title=2007 Newcomb Cleveland Prize Recipients|work=AAAS - The World's Largest General Scientific Society}}</ref> Light-directed combinatorial synthesis has been used by [[Stephen Fodor]] and coworkers at [[Affymetrix]] to make DNA arrays containing millions of different sequences for genetic analyses.

From 1975, Stryer authored ten editions of the textbook ''Biochemistry''.<ref>Latchman, D.S. (1995) ''Trends Biochem. Sci.'' 20:488.</ref>

Stryer also chaired a National Research Council committee that produced a report entitled ''Bio2010: Transforming Undergraduate Education for Future Research Biologists''.<ref>{{cite book|title=BIO2010: Transforming Undergraduate Education for Future Research Biologists - The National Academies Press|doi=10.17226/10497|pmid=20669482|year=2003|isbn=978-0-309-08535-9|last1=Council|first1=National Research|last2=Studies|first2=Division on Earth Life|last3=Sciences|first3=Board on Life|last4=Century|first4=Committee on Undergraduate Biology Education to Prepare Research Scientists for the 21st}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Points of View: Is Bio2010 the Right Blueprint for the Biology of the Future? | pmc=256982 | pmid=14673487 | doi=10.1187/cbe.03-10-0039 | volume=2 | issue=4 | year=2003 | journal=Cell Biol Educ | pages=224–7 | last1 = Kennedy | first1 = D}}</ref>
